nameStory: The 'stiff' in stiff marsh bedstraw refers to its upright stems that are more rigid than its sprawling relatives. Like other bedstraws, this plant was historically used to stuff mattresses and bedding, earning the whole family their cozy common name.
description: Stiff marsh bedstraw is a low-growing, sprawling herb that forms loose mats in wet areas. It has narrow, lance-shaped leaves arranged in whorls (circles) around square stems, creating a distinctive wheel-like pattern at each joint. The plant produces tiny white flowers and rarely grows taller than a foot or two, often reclining along the ground or leaning on other plants for support.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white flowers with only 3 petals instead of the usual 4 found in most bedstraws - count them carefully as this is the key feature that sets this species apart

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves arranged in whorls of 4-6 around the stem, feeling smooth to slightly rough when rubbed between your fingers

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Reclining or sprawling stems that are notably stiffer than other marsh bedstraws, often forming loose mats but not climbing aggressively

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Four-angled (square) stems that feel firm and somewhat rigid when gently bent, unlike the weak, clingy stems of catchweed bedstraw

habitat: Look for stiff marsh bedstraw in wet woods, marshy areas, along pond and stream shores, and in roadside ditches throughout New England. It thrives in moist to wet soils and can tolerate both sunny and partially shaded locations. You'll often find it mixed with sedges, rushes, and other wetland plants.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as the weather warms, with fresh green whorls of leaves appearing on square stems.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time when the diagnostic 3-petaled white flowers appear - this is the best time for positive identification.
seasonality.fall: Plants may persist into fall but become less noticeable as other vegetation dies back, though the square stems remain visible.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to the ground in most areas, leaving little trace until spring regrowth begins.

funFact: This humble wetland plant is considered a noxious weed in parts of the Northeast despite being completely native - it can form such dense mats in ideal conditions that it crowds out other plants and clogs waterways!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with three-petal bedstraw, which also has 3-petaled flowers but has much weaker, more delicate stems. Remember: stiff marsh bedstraw lives up to its name with noticeably firmer, more upright stems that don't flop over as easily.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being widespread and native, this species can be quite aggressive in ideal wetland conditions, which has led to its classification as a noxious weed in some areas - a reminder that even native plants can sometimes become problematic in certain contexts.
compareHints: Among the 15+ bedstraw species in New England, stiff marsh bedstraw is one of only two with 3-petaled flowers (the other being three-petal bedstraw). While catchweed bedstraw has sticky, grabby stems and common marsh bedstraw has weak, trailing stems, stiff marsh bedstraw strikes a middle ground with its notably firm but non-climbing growth habit.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's bedstraws, catchweed is unique for its extremely clingy nature and annual growth habit.

Hedge bedstraw differs from other common bedstraws by its smooth stems and purely white flowers - catchweed bedstraw has sticky stems, lady's bedstraw has yellow flowers, and fragrant bedstraw has a sweet vanilla scent when crushed.
Unlike its weedy cousin catchweed bedstraw which grabs onto your clothes with hooked bristles, sweet woodruff stays put and feels soft to touch.
Among New England's bedstraws, fragrant bedstraw is unique for its sweet vanilla scent when crushed – most other bedstraws are odorless or have different scents.
Among New England's 15+ bedstraw species, licorice bedstraw stands out with its consistently four broad, oval leaves per whorl - most others have 6-8 narrow, linear leaves arranged in circles.
Marsh-bedstraw is distinguished from other bedstraws by its preference for consistently wet habitats and its delicate, mat-forming growth pattern.
Lady's bedstraw stands out among New England's bedstraws because of its bright yellow flowers - most other bedstraw species have white or greenish blooms.
Among New England's bedstraws, rough bedstraw is distinguished by its prominent stem hooks and preference for wet areas.
Unlike catchweed bedstraw with its velcro-like sticky stems or sweet woodruff's hay-like fragrance, Torrey's wild licorice has smooth stems and that distinctive taste.
Unlike catchweed bedstraw which has sticky, grabby stems and four-petaled flowers, three-petal bedstraw feels smoother and has its distinctive three-petaled blooms.
Among New England's bedstraws, hairy bedstraw is unique for its consistently soft, fuzzy texture throughout the plant.

White bedstraw differs from other New England bedstraws by its upright growth habit and smooth stems - catchweed bedstraw has hooked bristles that grab onto clothing, while lady's bedstraw has bright yellow flowers instead of white.
Unlike the common catchweed bedstraw with its grabby, rough stems, boreal bedstraw is soft and non-sticky.
Northern bedstraw differs from other New England bedstraws by its upright growth habit and narrow leaves with three parallel veins.
Among New England's bedstraws, bluntleaf bedstraw stands out for its preference for wet habitats and those distinctive rounded leaf tips.
